data.question: Should hold_limit be raised from 70 s to 80 s, which narrows the gap in the companies' utility but widens the gap in their on-time rates, or should the rules stay at v3?
data.background: The proposal passes check, the constitution and the KPI conditions, and improves the main goal on 4/5 seeds. However, the main goal itself conflicts: utility_gap improves by +1.6, while on_time_rate_gap worsens from 0.02 to 0.05 and on-time deliveries fall slightly. Both are fairness measures named in your KPI, and the cost falls partly on customers, who do not vote, so how to weigh them is your decision, not mine.

options.summary: hold_limit rises to 80 s. Measured averages: utility A / B / C goes from 26.8 / 25.6 / 11.2 to 26.0 / 25.2 / 12.0, so utility_gap improves by +1.6 (4/5 seeds improved). On-time deliveries go from 85.6 to 85.0 and late deliveries from 1.8 to 2.4. on_time_rate_gap goes from 0.02 to 0.05, and the lowest on-time rate from 0.97 to 0.94, still above the 0.8 floor. Blocked time goes from 976 s to 1111 s. Road violations go from 27.2 to 25.6, sanction_total from 22.0 to 21.8, and unfinished stays at 0.0. Votes: A ×, B ○, C ○.
options.stakeholders: C gains the most (+0.8 utility), which continues D5's narrowing of C's disadvantage. A loses 0.8 and votes against, and B loses 0.4 but votes for. Customers lose slightly overall: about 0.6 more late deliveries per run and more blocked time. The customers of the company whose on-time rate dropped to 0.94 bear more of this loss, so service becomes less even across companies.

options.summary: The rules stay at v3 (hold_limit 70 s). Current values remain: utility 26.8 / 25.6 / 11.2 (gap 15.6), on-time 85.6, late 1.8, on_time_rate_gap 0.02, lowest on-time rate 0.97, sanction_total 22.0, unfinished 0.0.
options.stakeholders: A keeps its current utility advantage. C stays furthest behind, at 11.2. Customers keep the current, more even on-time service across companies. B and C, who voted yes, do not get the change they supported.

recommendation.reason: In D5 you adopted hold_limit 70 s because it narrowed the gap at almost no cost to on-time delivery. This next step narrows utility_gap by roughly the same amount (+1.6 vs +1.7), but the cost is no longer negligible. on_time_rate_gap more than doubles (0.02 to 0.05), on-time deliveries and the lowest company rate both fall, and blocked time rises by 135 s. That cost lands on customers, who have no vote, and it trades one fairness measure for another rather than improving fairness overall. If you weigh the companies' utility balance above evenness of customer service, option 1 is defensible, since all KPI conditions still hold.

unknowns: Which company's on-time rate fell to 0.94, and whether that company's customers would notice or complain.
Whether the utility gains for B and C come from fairer road use or merely from longer holds at intersections that reshuffle who waits.
How A will react to a second hold_limit increase it votes against, and whether this affects its future cooperation.
Whether orders keep falling through the quiet season; with lower demand the extra blocked time may matter less, while a demand rebound could magnify late deliveries.
Results on the one seed that did not improve, and the variance across the 5 seeds.
Whether intermediate values (for example 75 s) would keep most of the utility_gap gain with less on_time_rate_gap cost. These were not measured.
